newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland arms plan voted down at talks.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland arms plan voted down at talks.

text.p: Anglo-Irish proposals that Northern Ireland guerrillas should disarm while taking part in peace talks were defeated on Wednesday in a setback for attempts by London and Dublin to end decades of conflict.
"The governments' plans have been rejected. All three unionist parties voted against," David Adams of the Ulster Democratic Party told reporters.
The defeat, which Britain had expected, was assured when the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party voted with two smaller unionist groups against the plan.

Democratic Unionist Party leader Ian Paisley said: "We succeeded in what we set out to do -- to defeat the two governments' proposals called decommissioning but which were really non-decommissioning."
The proposal, a compromise after a year-long deadlock, said that loyalist and republican guerrillas should hand over some of their weapons during the talks in what it called parallel decommissioning.
But unionists feared that pro-British loyalists and their pro-Irish IRA foes would hang on to their weapons and wanted Britain to change the proposal to force guerrillas to disarm.

The Irish Republican Army called a ceasefire at the weekend to its 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland which will admit its political wing, Sinn Fein, to peace talks in six weeks' time.

Paisley's DUP and the small UK Unionist Party had said earlier that they would walk out of the talks altogether after Wednesday's vote in protest at what they called secret British attempts to appease the IRA and Sinn Fein.
Paisley said: "We are out of this process for good because this process is a failure and must be a failure because it is not a democratic process."

The result was made public soon after British Prime Minister Tony Blair told the London parliament that his government had made no change to its policy on guerrilla arms, despite unionist allegations that it had struck a deal with the IRA.
Britain proposed setting up an independent body on arms decommissioning to function alongside negotiations, starting in September, to end a conflict that has killed 3,200 since 1969.

"It is our desire to see decommissioning during the course of the negotiations. Indeed it is precisely for that reason that we have put in place a scheme whereby we will have an independent commission established," Blair said.
But unionists, who want the province to stay British, fear that the proposals were watered down to persuade the Irish Republican Army to declare the truce it called at the weekend.
The ceasefire will admit the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, to substantive talks in September if Britain deems the truce genuine.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, said earlier that she expected the "parallel decommissioning" proposal to be voted down.
"It's not a disaster, it is clearly a setback but no one ever said this would be easy," Mowlam told reporters a few hours before the mid-afternoon voting began.

Defeat leaves the single most contentious issue in a peace process started in December 1993 unresolved and throws into doubt plans to begin substantive negotiations on a lasting settlement by the two governments' target date of September 15.
Mowlam said that even if the proposals were voted down, the two governments would maintain their target date of September 15 to begin talks on a settlement.
But political sources said failure to agree how and when guerrillas should disarm might torpedo chances of getting the unionists and Sinn Fein to the same negotiating table.
Unionists say the IRA might abandon its truce, as it did a previous ceasefire called in August 1994, if the talks do not lead to the end of British rule.
